lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The Carbon Cycle: Stages and Processes

pages.body:
Every time you breathe out, you release carbon dioxide. Every time a plant photosynthesises, it absorbs carbon dioxide from the air. When wood burns, carbon that was stored in the tree for decades is released back into the atmosphere in minutes. When a leaf falls and rots on the forest floor, it too slowly releases carbon. The same carbon atoms have been cycling through living things, the atmosphere and the soil for hundreds of millions of years.

- Where does the carbon in your body come from?
- What do you think would happen to life on Earth if carbon dioxide disappeared from the atmosphere?
- Where do you think the carbon in petrol or charcoal originally came from?

lessons.title: The Carbon Cycle: Stages and Processes (part 2)

pages.body: > **DEFINITION** **Carbon cycle:** the continuous process by which carbon atoms are exchanged between the atmosphere, living organisms, soil, water and fossil fuel deposits. **Carbon dioxide (CO₂):** a gas in the atmosphere containing carbon. Plants absorb it in photosynthesis; it is released by respiration, combustion and decay. **Photosynthesis:** the process by which green plants use sunlight, CO₂ and water to produce glucose (food) and oxygen. Carbon is taken from the atmosphere and stored in the plant. **Respiration:** the process by which all living things release energy from food, producing CO₂ as a waste product. Carbon is returned to the atmosphere. **Combustion (burning):** the rapid reaction of a substance with oxygen, releasing energy, heat, light, CO₂ and water. Burning fuels releases stored carbon rapidly. **Decay (decomposition):** the breakdown of dead organic material by bacteria and fungi (decomposers), releasing CO₂eback into the atmosphere and nutrients into the soil.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The stages of the carbon cycle

pages.title: The stages of the carbon cycle
pages.body: The carbon cycle has no true beginning or end — it is a continuous loop of processes, each moving carbon from one reservoir to another. The main reservoirs of carbon are the atmosphere (as CO₂), living organisms (as organic molecules), soil (as humus and organic matter), fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas) and the ocean.

Photosynthesis is the entry point for most carbon into living systems. Green plants, algae and cyanobacteria absorb CO₂ from the atmosphere and use the energy from sunlight to convert it into glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆). This glucose is used for growth, forming the carbon-containing molecules — carbohydrates, proteins and fats — that make up all living matter. The overall process removes carbon from the atmosphere and stores it in plant tissue. Photosynthesis is sometimes called carbon fixation because it fixes atmospheric carbon into solid, organic compounds.

Respiration is carried out by all living organisms — plants, animals, fungi and bacteria — at all times, day and night. In cellular respiration, glucose is broken down using oxygen to release energy, producing CO₂ and water as waste products. This CO₂ is exhaled or released into the surrounding environment, returning carbon to the atmosphere. Plants carry out both photosynthesis and respiration, but during daylight the rate of photosynthesis usually exceeds respiration, so plants absorb more CO₂ than they release.

o: From living organisms to the atmosphere as CO₂
From the atmosphere into plant tissue as organic compounds

questions.e: All food chains begin with producers — green plants — that fix atmospheric carbon through photosynthesis, converting CO₂ into organic compounds such as glucose, starch and proteins.

questions.e: Plants carry out both photosynthesis and respiration, but during daylight the rate of photosynthesis usually exceeds respiration, so plants absorb more CO₂ than they release.

lessons.title: The Carbon Cycle: Stages and Processes (part 4)

pages.body: Burning (combustion) releases carbon that has been stored — either in living plant material (burning wood, charcoal or crop residues) or in ancient organic material transformed into fossil fuels (coal, oil and natural gas). Burning firewood releases carbon that was fixed by the tree over the past decades. Burning coal releases carbon that was fixed by ancient plants hundreds of millions of years ago. This is why burning fossil fuels is considered a major driver of climate change — it adds 'old' carbon to the atmosphere much faster than natural processes can remove it.

Decay and decomposition occur when organisms die and their bodies are broken down by decomposers — bacteria and fungi in the soil. As they break down organic matter into simpler substances, they release CO₂ into the atmosphere and mineral nutrients into the soil. Incomplete decay over millions of years, under conditions of heat and pressure, converts organic matter into coal, oil and natural gas — the fossil fuels.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Why the carbon cycle is a repeated pattern

pages.title: Why the carbon cycle is a repeated pattern
pages.body: The carbon cycle is described as a repeated pattern because the same carbon atoms cycle continuously through the environment. No carbon is permanently created or destroyed — it simply moves from one reservoir to another. Carbon that is in the atmosphere today as CO₂ might be absorbed by a tree tomorrow through photosynthesis, eaten by a caterpillar, breathed out by a bird, deposited in soil by a decomposer, and returned to the atmosphere — all within a few weeks. The same carbon atom might then remain locked in soil for centuries before being taken up by another plant.

pages.title: Word equations for the processes of the carbon cycle
pages.body:
- Photosynthesis. Carbon dioxide + water, with light energy and chlorophyll, gives glucose + oxygen.
- Respiration. Glucose + oxygen gives carbon dioxide + water + energy.
- Combustion. Fuel + oxygen gives carbon dioxide + water + heat energy.
- Decay. Decomposers feed on dead organisms and waste and release carbon dioxide as they respire.

Photosynthesis is the only one of these processes that removes carbon dioxide from the air. Respiration, combustion and decay all return carbon dioxide to the air. The amount of carbon dioxide in the air stays steady only when the amount removed balances the amount returned.

> **Lesson 1 Assessment**

questions.q: Why is the carbon cycle called a 'repeated pattern'?

Because all organisms respire at the same rate
questions.e: DEFINITION Carbon cycle: the continuous process by which carbon atoms are exchanged between the atmosphere, living organisms, soil, water and fossil fuel deposits.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The carbon cycle and the composition of air

pages.body:
Before the Industrial Revolution, the level of CO₂ in the atmosphere was about 280 parts per million (ppm). Today, because of burning fossil fuels, it has exceeded 420 ppm — the highest level in 3 million years. This extra carbon, once locked underground, is now in the atmosphere affecting weather patterns, ocean temperatures and rainfall around the world — including in Ghana.

- How does the level of CO₂ in the atmosphere affect the temperature of the Earth?
- Can you explain how a food chain connects to the carbon cycle?

pages.title: The carbon cycle and the composition of air
pages.body:
One of the most important roles of the carbon cycle is maintaining the balance of gases in the atmosphere. The atmosphere is a mixture of nitrogen (about 78%), oxygen (about 21%), CO₂ (about 0.04%) and other gases. The very small but critical proportion of CO₂ in the air is maintained by the carbon cycle.

Plants absorb CO₂ from the air during photosynthesis and release oxygen. All living things consume oxygen and release CO₂ during respiration. When the rate of photosynthesis across the globe equals the rate of respiration and other CO₂-releasing processes, the level of CO₂ in the atmosphere stays stable. The carbon cycle thus acts as a natural feedback mechanism, maintaining the atmospheric composition within a range that supports life.

questions.q: How does the carbon cycle help maintain the balance of gases in the atmosphere?
o: It converts all atmospheric nitrogen into CO₂
It ensures CO₂ levels are kept constant by balancing photosynthesis (absorbing CO₂) with respiration and burning (releasing CO₂)
It removes oxygen from the atmosphere to keep CO₂ levels stable
It produces all the nitrogen used by plants

questions.q: Before the Industrial Revolution, CO₂ in the atmosphere was about 280 ppm. Today it exceeds 420 ppm. What is the primary cause of this increase?
o: Increased respiration by a growing world population
Volcanic eruptions releasing stored CO₂
The burning of fossil fuels releasing ancient stored carbon
Increased photosynthesis by trees
questions.e: Burning (combustion) releases carbon that has been stored — either in living plant material (burning wood, charcoal or crop residues) or in ancient organic material transformed into fossil fuels (coal, oil and natural gas).

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The carbon cycle and food chains

pages.body: Disrupting this balance — for example by burning large amounts of fossil fuels or by destroying forests — releases CO₂ faster than photosynthesis can absorb it. This increases the concentration of CO₂ in the atmosphere, contributing to the enhanced greenhouse effect and global warming.

pages.title: The carbon cycle and food chains
pages.body: Every organism in a food chain contains carbon in its body, and the carbon cycle describes how that carbon moves through the chain. All food chains begin with producers — green plants — that fix atmospheric carbon through photosynthesis, converting CO₂ into organic compounds such as glucose, starch and proteins.

When a primary consumer (such as a grasshopper or cow) eats a plant, it takes in the carbon stored in the plant's tissues. Some of this carbon is used for energy through respiration and is returned to the atmosphere as CO₂. The rest is incorporated into the consumer's body. When a secondary consumer (such as a lizard eating a grasshopper, or a human eating beef) eats the primary consumer, the same process continues. At each level of the food chain, carbon is transferred upward through eating, and some is continuously returned to the atmosphere through respiration.

When any organism in the food chain dies, decomposers break down its body, releasing the remaining carbon as CO₂ into the atmosphere and as mineral nutrients into the soil. Nothing is wasted — all the carbon that was fixed by the plant at the start of the food chain eventually returns to the atmosphere.

questions.q: In a food chain, which organism is responsible for fixing atmospheric CO₂ into organic compounds?
o: Primary consumer (herbivore)
Secondary consumer (carnivore)
Decomposer
Producer (green plant)
questions.e: All food chains begin with producers — green plants — that fix atmospheric carbon through photosynthesis, converting CO₂ into organic compounds such as glucose, starch and proteins.

questions.q: When a grasshopper eats a maize plant, what happens to the carbon in the maize?

None of it reaches the grasshopper

lessons.title: Greenhouse gases and the carbon cycle

pages.body: Example of a food chain in Ghana with carbon flow: Maize plant → Grasshopper → Lizard → Hawk. The maize fixes atmospheric CO₂ during photosynthesis. The grasshopper eats the maize and respires, releasing some CO₂. The lizard eats the grasshopper and respires further. The hawk eats the lizard. When the hawk dies, decomposers return the remaining carbon to the atmosphere and soil.

pages.title: Greenhouse gases and the carbon cycle
pages.body: Greenhouse gases are gases in the atmosphere that absorb infrared radiation (heat) and prevent it from escaping into space, warming the Earth. The most important greenhouse gas linked to the carbon cycle is CO₂. Others include methane (CH₄), produced when organic matter decomposes without oxygen (in waterlogged soils, in the guts of cattle, in landfills), and nitrous oxide (N₂O) from fertilisers and soils.

The relationship between greenhouse gases and the carbon cycle is direct. Every time carbon is released from a living organism or from fossil fuels as CO₂, it adds to the greenhouse effect. The carbon cycle has a natural buffering capacity — oceans and forests absorb large amounts of CO₂, partly counteracting human emissions. But human activities are releasing carbon much faster than these natural sinks can absorb it.

When forests in Ghana are cut down and burned (deforestation), the carbon stored in the trees is released as CO₂ immediately from burning, and is no longer absorbed by photosynthesis once the trees are gone. This contributes to both increased greenhouse gas levels and reduced capacity to absorb future CO₂. Protecting Ghana's forests is therefore directly linked to controlling greenhouse gas levels.

> **Lesson 2 Assessment**

questions.q: CO₂ is described as a greenhouse gas because it:
o: Absorbs infrared radiation and prevents heat from escaping the Earth's atmosphere
Reflects sunlight away from the Earth, keeping it cool
Is the primary gas used in photosynthesis
Is produced only inside greenhouses
questions.e: Greenhouse gases are gases in the atmosphere that absorb infrared radiation (heat) and prevent it from escaping into space, warming the Earth.

questions.q: Deforestation in Ghana affects the carbon cycle because:
o: Trees produce CO₂, so cutting them reduces greenhouse gases
Cutting and burning trees releases stored carbon as CO₂ and removes photosynthetic capacity
Deforestation has no effect on the carbon cycle
Trees produce methane, so cutting them reduces the greenhouse effect

questions.q: Methane (CH₄) is produced in the carbon cycle when:

Organic matter decomposes without oxygen (anaerobically)
Photosynthesis occurs at night
Animals breathe oxygen
questions.e: Others include methane (CH₄), produced when organic matter decomposes without oxygen (in waterlogged soils, in the guts of cattle, in landfills), and nitrous oxide (N₂O) from fertilisers and soils.

questions.q: Why do oceans and forests help slow the increase in atmospheric CO₂ from human activities?
o: They reflect sunlight back into space
They act as carbon sinks — absorbing large amounts of CO₂ from the atmosphere
They produce methane that neutralises CO₂
They prevent the burning of fossil fuels
questions.e: The carbon cycle has a natural buffering capacity — oceans and forests absorb large amounts of CO₂, partly counteracting human emissions.

questions.q: Which of the following activities would most directly REDUCE the amount of CO₂ added to the atmosphere from the carbon cycle?
o: Clearing more forest to create farmland
Burning crop residues after harvest
Planting trees and protecting existing forests
Increasing the number of cattle on a farm

pages.body:
| **Word** | **What it means** |
|---|---|
| Carbon cycle | The continuous process by which carbon atoms move between the atmosphere, living organisms, soil, water and fossil fuels |
| Photosynthesis | Process by which plants use CO₂, water and sunlight to make glucose; removes carbon from the atmosphere |
| Respiration | Process by which organisms break down glucose to release energy, releasing CO₂ |
| Combustion | Burning; the rapid reaction of a substance with oxygen, releasing CO₂ and energy |
| Decay (decomposition) | Breakdown of dead organic matter by bacteria and fungi, releasing CO₂ and nutrients |
| Carbon fixation | The conversion of atmospheric CO₂ into solid organic compounds by photosynthesis |
| Fossil fuels | Coal, oil and natural gas; formed from ancient organic matter; burning them releases stored carbon |
| Food chain | A sequence of organisms in which each is eaten by the next; carbon passes along the chain |
| Producer | An organism (green plant) that makes its own food by photosynthesis; starts all food chains |
| Greenhouse gas | A gas (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O) that absorbs infrared radiation and warms the atmosphere |
| Deforestation | The clearing of forests; releases stored carbon and reduces photosynthetic capacity |
| Carbon sink | A natural reservoir (ocean, forest) that absorbs and stores more carbon than it releases |
